🌱 Basics · Lesson 2 · 2 min read

Machine Learning

How computers learn from examples instead of instructions.

Learning from examples

Machine learning (ML) is the most common way to build AI today. Instead of programming every rule, we give the computer lots of examples, and it finds the patterns by itself. To build a spam filter, for example, you show it thousands of emails labelled “spam” or “not spam”. It starts to notice clues: words like “FREE!!!”, strange links or unknown senders.

Training and testing

Learning happens step by step. During training, the model guesses an answer, measures how wrong it was (the error) and adjusts itself a tiny bit to be less wrong. This repeats thousands or even millions of times. Then comes testing: the model gets new examples it has never seen, to check that it really learned the pattern instead of just memorising the answers.

Did you know? When a model memorises its training examples but fails on new ones, it's called overfitting — like learning test answers by heart without understanding the topic.

Three ways to learn

Supervised learning: every example comes with the right answer (a label), like photos tagged “cat” or “dog”. Unsupervised learning: there are no labels, and the model finds groups by itself, like sorting songs by how similar they sound. Reinforcement learning: the model learns by trial and error, getting rewards for good moves — that's how AI learned to play Go and many video games.

Data is everything

A model is only as good as its data. If the examples are too few, messy or one-sided, the model learns the wrong pattern. Imagine a model that learns to recognise wolves, but every wolf photo in its training data has snow in the background. It might decide that snow means “wolf” — and call a husky in the snow a wolf!

Key points

  • Machine learning models learn patterns from examples (data) instead of hand-written rules.
  • Training: guess, measure the error, adjust, repeat. Testing: check on new, unseen data.
  • Too little or one-sided data makes the model learn the wrong lessons.

Check yourself

Why do we test a model on examples it has never seen before?

Show the answer

Right answer: To check it learned the pattern, not just memorised the answers

A model that only memorised its training data fails on anything new. Testing on unseen data shows whether it really learned the general pattern.
